Two dominant, easily quantified chemotypes in the full clean set: (a) adamantyl-containing compounds, motif 'C12CC3CC', 448/3,028 (14.8%); (b) acyl-piperidin-4-yl ureas, motif 'NC1CCN(C(=O)', 57 compounds.

Chemotype-level comparison of measured activity (mean / median pChEMBL) shows the urea-acyl-piperidine series is markedly potency-enriched versus the broad adamantyl series: acyl-piperidin-4-yl ureas, 55 measured, mean 8.88, median 9.11 (IQR 8.65-9.40); adamantyl-containing compounds, 430 measured, mean 7.59, median 7.80.

Assays/documents: 525 unique assays across 237 documents (ChEMBL). Assay types retained: binding (B) and functional (F). Organism: Homo sapiens. Mechanism filter: none.

The human sEH chemical space in ChEMBL is a moderately large (3,028 compounds), potency-dense but structurally uneven set, concentrated around two to three urea-based chemotypes. Density and potency are decoupled: the most populated regions are not the most potent, and the most potent compounds live in thinly populated regions of the map.

Evidence discipline: all potency, ranking, and active/inactive statements above are backed by measured pChEMBL values from the retrieved clean table and the GTM node-level activity landscape CSV, not by node density or scaffold counts. Dense nodes and their scaffolds are reported as structural observations only.

Limitations: (1) node-level activity values are means over few compounds in sparse nodes and can be noisy; (2) the activity landscape was rendered as a regression (continuous pChEMBL) landscape because the dataset's activity mapping is regression - a binary active/inactive classification landscape was not generated by the tool, so active/inactive counts were computed directly from the pChEMBL >= 6 threshold instead; (3) curation filters (judge-based keyword/metadata filtering plus standardization) removed ~3,151 suspicious raw rows, which could bias the set toward well-annotated sEH assays.
